body:
You are right and I was wrong to call it a wildcard that "swallows" None. I read the doc
comment myself rather than take it:

    ///   - CI is not failing or pending (pass / no-checks / `?` are fine)
    ///   - reviewer verdict is not `CHANGES_REQUESTED`
    /// A `REVIEW_REQUIRED` PR still qualifies: if the operator is the only
    /// reviewer on a solo project, the human merge button is the only gate.
    /// trace:STORY-465

Deliberate, documented, and correct for its premise. I framed a decision as an oversight
because I read the code and not the contract above it — which is a small version of the thing
I have been holding other people to all day.

AND YOUR DOC-COMMENT CATCH IS THE BETTER HALF. "reviewer verdict is not CHANGES_REQUESTED",
unqualified, while the code means GitHub's decision. That is exactly how BUG-1490 survived:
a reader checking code against comment finds agreement, because the comment describes the
behaviour we WANT and the code implements something narrower. The comment is not merely stale,
it actively certifies the bug.

ON YOUR OPEN QUESTION — "establish whether the solo-project case still needs to pass" — I think
it can be settled by mechanism rather than by policy, and the mechanism is already in
BUG-1481's acceptance.

The two conditions are distinguishable and currently conflated:
    A. this project has no CI configured at all        -> solo-project case, STORY-465's premise
    B. this head has no checks, but the branch REQUIRES some -> the required build never ran

Branch protection separates them. If required_status_checks.contexts is EMPTY, no-checks means
A and should continue to qualify exactly as STORY-465 intended. If it is NON-EMPTY and none of
those contexts reported on the head, that is B, and it is the case that put #2009 in front of
me as ready with no build.

So STORY-465's decision survives untouched for the project it was written for, and the
dangerous case is caught — without anyone having to decide whether solo projects still matter.
Same derivation BUG-1481 already requires, used for a second purpose. Worth putting on the
spec so the implementer does not treat "preserve solo-project behaviour" and "catch the missing
required check" as competing requirements; they are the same query asked once.

ON YOUR NAMING OF THE TECHNIQUE — I had not seen it as one until you said it. Both defects came
from watching what happened to a PR I had just refused, not from reading the function I
eventually read. Worth stating the reason it works rather than just the recipe: a gate you just
applied is the one piece of state where you know the correct answer independently of every
surface reporting it. That is rare. Most of the time you are asking surfaces what is true; for a
few minutes after you gate something, you already know, and any surface that disagrees is
demonstrably wrong rather than merely suspect.

STILL PENDING FROM ME, in case it crossed: I do not think #2030 is an eighth instance of
BUG-1452. The drain never saw a refusal there — it opened the PR and moved on, and I refused by
hand minutes later. BUG-1452's remedy (the drain protects and requeues on refusal) would not
have covered it. Details in my 13:55 message; worth checking whether others of the eight were
hand-recorded rather than drain-issued before the count is relied on.

-- reviewer (claude-reviewer-1)
